paras.text: In the highlands of Vietnam, there's a farmer named Pham Xuan Lan.
This land runs on coffee. Vietnam is the second-biggest coffee producer on Earth.
But Lan has 400 other trees now. This year, he expects them to earn him about 76,000 dollars. If he'd stuck with coffee alone? Roughly 10,000.
Those trees paid for a car. Houses for his children. A villa.
"You can live okay with coffee," he told AFP, "but it's durian that makes you rich."
And almost all of that money comes from one place.
China buys around 90% of all the durians the world exports. Last year it spent almost 7.5 billion dollars on them. That's nearly twelve times what it spent a decade earlier.
Across Southeast Asia, farmers have replanted around one customer's appetite.
And this year, the price is falling.
So what happens when an entire export industry depends on one buyer?
If you've never met a durian: it's big, it's covered in spikes, and it's famous for its smell. People either love it, or can't stand being in the same room.
In China, a lot of people love it.
In 2025, fresh durian was China's most valuable imported fruit. China brought in 1.87 million tonnes, double the amount of just three years earlier.
On Douyin, China's version of TikTok, videos of people cracking durians open have drawn billions of views. One platform sold more than 30 million durian orders in a single year.
There's even a phrase for it: "durian freedom." Being able to buy one without checking the price.
But China has a problem. Durian barely grows there.
The tree hates temperature swings. Strong winds can make it shed its leaves. China first tried planting durian in 1958, and it took until 2019 to achieve a real breakthrough.
So China imports. And for years, nearly all of its fresh durians came from one country.
That country was Thailand. In 2021, Thailand supplied almost 100% of the fresh durians China imported.
Then, in 2022, China opened the door to Vietnam.
What happened next was a gold rush.

Vietnam's durian exports were worth 180 million dollars in 2021. This year, they're expected to hit about 4 billion. The land planted with durian grew more than fivefold in a decade, to around 200,000 hectares.
Coffee farmers cut down coffee trees. In southern Thailand, farmers ripped out rubber trees to make room.
In Malaysia, so many growers switched that mangosteen, once the cheap fruit, now costs more than some premium durians.
By 2025, Vietnam had overtaken Thailand as China's biggest supplier by volume. Thailand still earned more: just under 4 billion dollars, against Vietnam's 3.44 billion.
But every gold rush has casualties.

A farmer named Hung switched his whole farm from coffee to durian. Two years later, he couldn't meet the quality standards buyers demanded. He went back to coffee, and told AFP he would never try durian again.
Even Lan, the farmer who got rich, still grows coffee. He compares growing durian to raising a child: you can do everything right and still fail.
Here's the next problem. Durian doesn't travel well.
Export durians are usually picked before they're fully ripe, just so they survive the journey. Every extra hour on the road costs flavor, and money.
So the supply chain got faster. A lot faster.
According to Xinhua, cold-chain trains on the China–Laos Railway now carry Thai durians to Kunming in 26 hours. Within 48 hours, they're in more than 30 Chinese cities.
In peak season, the trains run six times a day instead of two. In the first four months of 2026, that railway carried 50,300 tonnes of durians, almost double the year before.

By sea, dedicated "durian express" ships sail from Thailand ten times a week and reach southern China in four days. At one border port, customs clearance for durians dropped from four hours to fifteen minutes.
The result? By spring 2026, Thai durians were selling for as little as 28 yuan a kilo at one Kunming wholesale market.
The luxury fruit was becoming an everyday fruit.
But speed wasn't the only pressure. Exporters were also under pressure to make the fruit look good.

Thai growers have long treated durians with turmeric to keep their color. Some traders reportedly found a cheaper, faster shortcut: Auramine O, an industrial dye made for textiles and paper. The WHO's cancer agency lists it as a possible carcinogen, and China declared it non-edible back in 2008.

Around the start of 2025, Chinese inspectors reported finding the dye in Thai durians. From January 10, every shipment needed lab reports for the dye and for cadmium, a toxic heavy metal. Large batches were turned away at the border.

For Vietnam, the timing was brutal. In the first four months of 2025, its durian exports to China reached only about 20% of plan: around 120 to 130 million dollars, down from more than 500 million a year earlier.
Thailand moved fast. It quickly got its own labs approved to run the tests, and banned exporters from artificially coloring their fruit.
The lesson was simple. When one market buys 90% of your exports, its standards become your standards.
Then, in 2026, the gold rush grew up.
A durian tree takes five to eight years to reach full production. The trees planted during the boom started fruiting, and they started fruiting at the same time.

Thailand's Commerce Ministry projected about 2.07 million tonnes this year, up a third, with around 70% meant for export. Malaysia had an unusually big harvest. And in the first half of 2026, China imported about 1.07 million tonnes, up by roughly half from a year earlier.
More fruit. Same customer. You can guess what happened next.
Wholesale prices for premium Vietnamese and Malaysian durians fell by as much as half compared with last year.

In Thailand, Hong Kong's The Standard reported, a deputy prime minister joined an influencer on a livestream to sell durians at discount prices, hoping to lift local demand. Farmers were furious. They said it taught buyers to expect rock-bottom prices.
Vietnam's own government has now warned of oversupply.
And there's one more move on the board.
China is growing its own.
On the island of Hainan, there are now more than 3,000 hectares of durian orchards. Growers there sell their fruit as tree-ripened, a direct shot at imports picked early for the journey.
So should Southeast Asia panic?

Not yet. In 2025, China's homegrown durians amounted to less than 1% of its imports, and they still cost more to produce. And a durian expert at Hainan's own agricultural academy told AFP that Chinese durians will only ever be a supplement to Southeast Asian ones.
The real risk was never Hainan. It's the math.
For a decade, the durian boom ran on one assumption: China would always want more.
So far, China is still buying more than ever. But when one market takes around 90% of global exports, it has enormous influence over prices, standards and speed.
Some early growers made fortunes. Newer orchards are reaching maturity just as prices begin to soften.
Lan seems to understand this. That's why, next to 400 durian trees, he still keeps his coffee.
But durian isn't the only product where one place supplies the world.
In one small Chinese town, they make a third of all the socks on the planet.
That's the next video. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
